user_prompt:
These 2 questions belong together and follow one another in the test booklet.

## Question 1

There are 10 girls and 20 boys in Juanita's class. Juanita said that there is one girl for every two boys. Her friend Amanda said that means 1/2 of all the students in the class are girls.

How many students are there in Juanita's class?
Answer: ____

Is Juanita right? Answer: ____
Use words or pictures to explain why.

## Question 2

There are 10 girls and 20 boys in Juanita's class. Juanita said that there is one girl for every two boys. Her friend Amanda said that means 1/2 of all the students in the class are girls.

How many students are there in Juanita's class?
Answer: ____

Is Amanda right? Answer: ____
Use words and pictures to explain why.

Answer each of the 2 questions.

answer_1.title: Answer 1

answer_2.description: Your answer to question 2, as you would write it in the test booklet, with any work, explanation, or description of a drawing that the question asks for.
answer_2.title: Answer 2

output.answer_1: There are 30 students in Juanita's class (10 girls + 20 boys = 30). Is Juanita right? Yes. For every 2 boys there is 1 girl: the 20 boys form 10 groups of 2 boys, and each group pairs with 1 girl, and there are 10 girls, so 10 girls correspond to 20 boys, one girl for every two boys. Picture: draw 10 groups, each with one girl (G) and two boys (B): G B B, G B B, ... repeated 10 times, giving 10 G and 20 B.
output.answer_2: There are 30 students in Juanita's class (10 girls + 20 boys = 30). Is Amanda right? No. Half of the 30 students would be 15 girls, but there are only 10 girls. Girls are 10 out of 30, which is 1/3 of the class, not 1/2. Picture: draw 30 squares in a row; shade 10 of them for girls. The shaded part is one third of the whole, and 15 squares would be needed to show one half. Saying one girl for every two boys describes the ratio of girls to boys, not the fraction of all students who are girls.
